en: I worship that supreme reality, the embodiment of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) made known by the Tripurātāpinī-vidyā, which in essence is of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Worshipful Ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, we have offered praise; may we attain the life-span ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya with his unharmed wheel grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!

Hariḥ Oṃ. Now, in this interval, the Blessed One, having assumed the form of the Lord of Prajāpati which is Vaiṣṇava and the cause of dissolution, [becomes] the Goddess named Tripurā through such powers as these. By means of the syllable *Hīṃ*, which consists of Hara and Māyā, the Goddess known as Hṛllekhā reaches the three cities—the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, namely heaven, earth, and the netherworld—at the end of the three peaks in the abode of dissolution, the radiant and formidable dwelling.
She alone is proclaimed as this Goddess Tripurā.
[We meditate upon] that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ.

May he who impels our thoughts, who is beyond the realm of dust—svāhā! Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; he knows how to burn away those who act with hostility. May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses a river in a boat, beyond all misfortunes.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May He deliver me from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality.
The hundred-syllabled mantra is the supreme knowledge, consisting of the three Vedas; it is the eight-syllabled Tripura, the Supreme Goddess.
The first four words expand upon the Supreme Brahman;
the second group is called Śakti;
the third group pertains to Śiva.

In this regard, the arrangement is explained as follows: the worlds, the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the codes of dharma, the medical sciences, and the celestial luminaries [all arise] from the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Now we shall explain its supreme, profound mystery, which is the source of the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa);
that is the eternal Brahman.

The Supreme Lord is without characteristics, untainted, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of mental affliction; He is the God who unfolds, perceives, expands, and desires the state of pure consciousness.
That one God, whose form is Śiva, unfolds as the object of perception, and He desires [to manifest] among ascetics, sacrifices, and yogis.

Granted, this very Nirañjana arises; by way of desirelessness, he unfolds. He creates the letters *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*. Therefore, the Lord is designated as Kāma. By that convention, Kāma pervades the letter *ka*.
"Kāma eva idam tat-tat"—the letter *ka* is grasped here; "bhasma" is the meaning of that word (*tat*). He who knows this [attains it].
In the phrase "savitur vareṇyam," the root *ṣūṅ* means "the procreation of living beings"; Savitṛ procreates, brings forth, and generates power in living beings.

This primordial Śakti Tripurā, the supreme goddess Mahākuṇḍalinī, gives birth [to all]. Whoever studies the circle of Jātavedas (fire) is pervaded by everything. The single Śakti of the triangle brings forth through the highly auspicious letter *E*.
Therefore, only the letter *e* is grasped.
It is the most excellent (*vareṇya*), the best, the one worthy of worship, the imperishable (*akṣara*), and the one to be saluted.
Therefore, he who knows thus grasps the letter *e*, which is the most excellent.
We shall explain the phrase "bhargo devasya dhīmahi" as follows:
the letter *dha* signifies support (*dhāraṇā*).
By means of the intellect (*dhī*), the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, is supported.
The divine *bhargas* is the intermediate [syllable], the fourth vowel (*akṣara*), which is directly the Fourth (*turīya*), all-encompassing, and existing within all.
They explain the form of *bhargas* as being the syllable *ī*, the fourth vowel, which stands in the middle of the words;
therefore, in the phrase "we meditate upon the divine *bhargas*," the syllable *ī* is understood.
The explanation of the word *mahī* is as follows: that in which greatness (*mahattva*), inertia (*jaḍatva*), and hardness (*kāṭhinya*) exist is *mahi*; this is the letter *la*, the supreme abode.
That which is rich in hardness, together with the oceans, the mountains, the seven continents, and the forests—a radiant form—is declared by the letter *la* to be the very mandala itself.
By the phrase "the goddess Earth is *mahī*," they explain it thus.
"May He who impels our intellects.

The Supreme Self, Sadāśiva, the primordial and transcendent source, is the self in the form of a *jyotir-liṅga* represented by the letter *la*, which has become fixed (*sthāṇu*). One should meditate upon Him by contemplating with the mind alone—free from vocal utterance—the thought: "May He impel (*pracodayāt*) our intellects (*dhiyaḥ*), our cognitions, toward the supreme reality, which is free from the desire for meditation and beyond conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). Thus one should contemplate.

"Beyond the *rajas*, [is] *sāvadom*"; at the conclusion of that, the supreme, stainless light, the deity within the heart, consciousness, the mark of *cit*—[all this] is clearly explained as the five-syllabled *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, which dwells in the temple of the heart, which begins with *hṛllekhā*, which generates the five elements, and which consists of five *kalās*.
He who knows thus.
Now, they say that the supreme *kāma-kūṭa* is composed of the *kāmakalā*.

Having recited the thirty-two syllables beginning with *tat savitur vareṇyam*, [the text states]: "The syllable *tat* is the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva; by means of establishing identity (*tādātmya*) through the absence of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), the syllable *ha*—which is the form of Śiva—is inscribed as the syllable-less syllable.
Taking up the exclusion of that which is external (*parāgvṛtti*), it reveals the Power (*śakti*).

Having inscribed the moonlight below the sun by means of the preceding path, it says: "They declare that which resides from the base (*mūla*) to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) to be the syllable-less, non-dual [reality]. Thus, it speaks of the Blessed Lord, the God who has arisen as the very essence of Śiva and Śakti.
This Śiva is the supreme deity, and this Śakti is born from the living soul;
through the union of the sun and the moon, the state of Haṃsa is said to arise. || 1 ||
From that, desire unfolds; from desire comes the supreme Śiva.
This Kārṣṇa is this Kāmadeva; he is called the most excellent Bharga. || 2 ||

The *bharga* of that *savitṛ*, the divine, is the milk to be poured forth; it is the imperishable syllable that destroys the honey. Through the union of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the individual self (*jīvātman*), the third syllable *tat* is clearly manifest, and *hi* is that very same [union]. Thus, the first deity, the stainless Sadāśiva, explains the final syllable.

The syllable *dhi* signifies the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*) and its retention; *mahī* signifies the retention of inertness (*jaḍatva*). The letter *la* is beneath *śiva*; thus the meaning of the letter *la* is clear. The final syllable is the supreme consciousness (*paramaṃ caitanyam*), which "may He impel our intellects" (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*), beyond the realm of passion (*paro rajase*), ending with *svāhā*. Such is the *kūṭa*, the abode of the digit of desire (*kāmakalālaya*), the transformer of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaparivartaka*), the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. And the Blessed Lord [attains this] for whoever knows it thus. Now, from this, one proceeds to the other, the third *kūṭa*, that of Śakti.

By means of the thirty-two-syllable Gāyatrī mantra, "tatsaviturvareṇyam," it is shown that from that Self (Ātman) arises space (ākāśa), and from space, wind (vāyu) vibrates; dependent upon that is the "vareṇya" (the most excellent), which is the emerging Savitṛ. From this, the individual soul (jīvātman) arises as the supreme self (paramātman), and clearly attains that syllable of the individual soul (jīvākṣara) whose nature is the power of illumination (prakāśa-śakti). By the words "bhargo devasya dhīmahi," the syllable of the nature of Śiva, who is the support, is enumerated.
By the words beginning with "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt," the entire desirable, delightful, and visible aggregate of power (śakti-kūṭa) is made manifest.
Thus, whoever studies this fifteen-syllable mantra of Tripura attains all desires;
he conquers all worlds;
he causes all speech to unfold.
He attains the state of Rudra;
having pierced through the abode of Viṣṇu, he attains the supreme Brahman—
so it is for one who knows thus.
Having thus declared this primary Vidyā, [the text states: "The Śaktikūṭa of this [Vidyā], beginning with Śakti-Śiva, is this Lopāmudrā.
In the second station (dhāman), the Hṛllekhā, which is the Śakti-bhūta, is devoid of the Bindu and is presided over by the Sage Krodha.
In the third station, by means of that very Vāgbhava-kūṭa of the aforementioned Vidyā, they declare the Mānavī, Cāndrī, and Kauberī Vidyās."
Below Madana is Śiva, who consists of Vāgbhava; above that is that which consists of Kāmakalā;
and above Śakti is Śakti—this is the Mānavī Vidyā.
In the fourth abode, there is another third [form] called Śiva-Śakti, and this is the lunar Vidyā.
In the fifth abode, this lunar [Vidyā] is to be meditated upon as Kāmādhāḥ-Śivādyakāmā.
That very same one is explained as Kauberī in the sixth abode.
He who knows thus:
having set aside the letter *e* and the fourth vowel (*au*), at the beginning of all [mantras], there is the one known as Vāgīśvarī or Agastya by means of the Sun and Moon.

In the seventh station, taking the third [letter] of this very aforementioned [mantra] beginning with *kāma*, doubling it, and placing *ka* below; then the seed-syllable of Śakti beginning with the digit of Madana (*madanakalā*); and the beginning of Vāgbhava—having made these two half-headed, this is the Nandividyā.

In the eighth *dhāman*, this is the *vidyā* known as *Prabhākarī*, consisting of the *vāgbhava* [syllable], the *āgastya*, that which consists of the parts of speech and meaning, the one called *kāmakalā*, the *sakala*, and the power of *māyā*.

Furthermore, in the ninth *dhāman*, there is again the *āgastya* and the *vāgbhava*; [this] *ṣaṇmukhī vidyā* is the abode of Śakti, Manmatha, Śiva-Śakti, Manmatha, and the Earth; it is the abode of Māyā, Kāmakalā, the Moon, the Sun, Anaṅga, Dhūrjaṭi, and Mahimā.

"In the tenth station, having again recited the Agastya-vidyā as illuminated by the Vidyā, and having again recited this final Māyā; in the eleventh station, having again recited Agastya, and having made the Vāgbhava of this very [Māyā], which is born of the thunderbolt (dhanaja) and the abode of the Kāmakalā, its innate form, and having recited the Śakti-kūṭa-rāja of Lopāmudrā—they declare this to be the Vaiṣṇavī-vidyā in the twelfth station.
He who knows thus.
He said to them:

O Blessed One, having heard all of this, you have made manifest and placed within your heart the supreme Vidyā known as Kāmā—the ancient one, whose form is the fourth (turīya), yet transcends the fourth (turīyātītā), most exalted, seated upon the seat of all mantras, surrounded by the deities of the primary and secondary seats (pīṭha-upapīṭha), pervading all arts (kalās), accompanied by fragrance, pollen, the heart-mantra, nectar, and all the senses; she who is eternally risen, the supreme, the Trikūṭā Tripurā, the highest Māyā, the most excellent Vaiṣṇavī. Having realized her and caused her to go to the abode-less state, [you have attained liberation].
Having placed within the pericarp of the heart-lotus the supreme Goddess Lakṣmī, who is Māyā, eternally arisen, the great bringer of subjugation, and the one who causes intoxication with passion;

One should meditate upon the Goddess Mahātripurā, the supreme Bhairavī who is the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), residing within the Śrīpīṭha at the center of the Tripīṭha, by means of the yoga of great meditation; she is known thus—this is the Great Upaniṣad. Thus ends the first Upaniṣad. 1.
Then, having recited "Now, therefore, for Jātavedas let us press the Soma," and so forth, the manifestation of Traipura is perceived.

Regarding the single-verse hymn beginning with "For Jātavedas," the sages said, "Explain the form of the ocean of seed-syllables that is dissolved within those positions—at its beginning, middle, and end.

The Blessed One said to them: "Regarding 'For Jātavedas let us press the Soma,' one should recite that [mantra] in reverse order. By taking the first [syllable] of the first [part] and making it long, and by using the first [syllable] of the second, 'sunavāma somam' (let us press the Soma), they declare this to be the Kaula, Vāma, and supreme Soma, which is great good fortune."

Having performed the purification of the hands (*karasuddhi*) by means of [the visualization of] the first as the cause of cessation (*nivṛtti*), the second as the cause of maintenance (*sthiti*), and the third as the cause of emanation (*sarga*)—which constitutes all perfections—and having clarified the *Tripurā-vidyā* by reciting "We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas" (*jātavedase sunavāma somam*) and so forth, they declare the *Mahāvidyeśvarī* mantra to be *Tripureśvarī*, beginning with "Jātavedasa.
The meaning of the sentence is that within the head of the first syllable of the *Mātṛkā*, there is the *Kuṇḍalinī* in the form of nectar and in the form of a triangle.
Thus, the first [syllable] is the primordial *Vāgbhava*.
The second is the abode of the arts of desire (*kāmakalālaya*).
By the word "born" (*jāta*), the unfolding of the Supreme Self is indicated.
Through the phrase beginning with "born," the Supreme Self is called Śiva.
They explain the full [mantra] beginning with "As soon as he is born, the desirer desires desire," and so forth.
That very [mantra], mounted upon the *gotra*, clarifies the mantra-syllables by means of the vowel situated in the middle of the nectar.
By the words "In the *gotra*," meaning "in the lineage of names" (*nāmagotra*), the abode of the *kāmakalā* is made clear; the remainder is explained by the words "the left," and so forth.
They explain that this Vidyā, which provides all protection, [is recited] by the eastern path.

Having thus clarified the Vidyā of Tripureśī with the mantra beginning with *jātavedasaḥ*, and having granted the fourth boon—either through the mantra *jāto deva eka īśvaraḥ* or *paramo jyotiḥ*—and having established the station of the Bindu as the full light (*pūrṇajyotiḥ*), and having connected the first, second, and third [syllables] with the relationship of "all-protecting" (*sarvarakṣākarī*), and having clarified the Vidyā in the form of the seat of the Self (*ātmāsana*), one recites the mantra beginning with *jātavedase sunavāma somaṃ*, remembers the protective Vidyā at the beginning and end of the two abodes (*dhāman*).
Having applied [the mantra] whose form consists of Śakti and Śiva, one should understand that "sa" is the syllable consisting of Śakti and "soma" is the abode (dhāma) consisting of Śiva.
He who knows this becomes fortunate.

Thus, one should know Tripuravāsinī, seated upon the throne of the Cakra, eternally risen, whose nature is the essence of Śiva and Śakti; she is Jātavedas, she is Śiva, and she is the syllable whose nature is Śakti. She exists within the interval between Śiva and Śakti, moving through the three peaks (trikūṭa), saluting the sun and the moon, and seated upon the throne of the Mantra—she is Tripura Mahālakṣmī.

Having clarified that which is eternally arisen, and having recited "We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas" and so forth; having first recalled the Vidyā in the form of the seat of the Eternal Self (Sadātmā), and having placed above it the Bindu which rises continuously throughout the day by means of the mantra beginning with "Veda"; and having clarified Tripurā Mālinī seated upon the Siddhāsana by reciting "We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas" and so forth; one should take refuge in Tripurā Sundarī, contemplate her as the syllables and letters, and [worship] Tripurā, who has become manifest as a form, whose very nature is form, and who is the Sovereign of all Vidyās.
Having clarified the Vidyā by reciting "jātavedase" and so forth, and having resorted to Tripurā-Lakṣmī, one should burn the fire;
reflecting that "she herself blazes within the mouth of Agni," one should clarify the Vidyā of the Sovereign Mother Tripurā, who is the triple light.
In this manner, by means of this [mantra], she who illumines the beyond—beginning with "sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi viśvā"—should be made manifest as the inner self (pratyagbhūtā).
They explain that this *vidyā* is for the rites of invocation and is firm in every respect.
Thus they explain this group of eight *vidyās* as being constituent parts of the goddess Mahāmāyā.

The gods indeed said to the Blessed One, "Tell us of the leader of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*), which fulfills all desires, is to be propitiated by all, possesses all forms, faces every direction, and is the door to liberation—sitting upon which yogis pierce the Supreme Brahman and enter into *nirvāṇa*."
The Blessed One said to them: "We shall explain the Śrīcakra.

Having drawn a triangle (trikoṇa) and a trident (tryasra), one should draw a measuring-stick line within its center; having extended it widely and formed a yoni at the front, and having made a measuring-stick line shaped like the front of the previous yoni, and having extended that all the way to the top and formed a yoni, the first triangle becomes the Cakra. The second becomes the intermediate space."

The third [wheel] is marked with eight *yoni*s. Then, having drawn a line from the front of each corner at the beginning and end of the eight-spoked wheel, and having drawn a line bound for the attraction of the target (*sādhya*) and so forth, one thus forms an upper *saṃpuṭa-yoni* mark; then, having drawn four upward lines from the flanks, there arises by successive order a wheel marked with ten *yoni*s using two measuring rods.
In this very same manner, there further arises a ten-spoked wheel.

Having joined the four lines at the tips of the middle triangle to the tips of the corner angles, and having drawn a measuring-line (mānayaṣṭi) reduced by one-tenth of those ten-spoked sections, a fourteen-spoked wheel is formed.
From that, a wheel enclosed by eight petals arises;
a wheel enclosed by sixteen petals has four gates.
Then there is the earthly wheel (*pārthiva-cakra*) with four doors.
Thus the wheel has been explained by way of the yoga of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-yoga*).
Alternatively, I shall describe the ninefold wheel in reverse order.
The first wheel is the Enchanter of the Three Worlds (Trailokyamohana). It consists of the eight [powers] beginning with Aṇimā; it consists of the eight measures (mātrās);
and it consists of the ten [powers] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
It becomes manifest;
it becomes presided over by Tripurā;
it becomes endowed with the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā.
The second is the wheel that fulfills all desires;
it consists of the sixteen [goddesses] beginning with Sakāmā who attract [beings],
and it is well-guarded.
It becomes presided over by Tripureśvarī. It is graced by the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā. It is the third wheel, the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa (the All-Agitating).
It consists of the eight [deities] beginning with Sānaṅgakusumā;
it is most secret;
it is presided over by Tripurasundarī.
It is endowed with the Sarvākarṣiṇī mudrā;
it is the fourth wheel, the bestower of all good fortune,
consisting of the twenty-eight [deities] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
It is accompanied by the oral tradition;
it is presided over by Tripuravāsinī;
and it is endowed with the Sarvavaśaṅkarī mudrā.
The wheel extending to the fourth state is the accomplisher of all aims; it is the group of ten beginning with the bestower of all supernatural powers;
it is the entirety of Kaula.
It is presided over by Tripurā Mahālakṣmī;
it is endowed with the Mahonmādinī mudrā;
it is the sixth wheel, which brings about all protection.
It becomes endowed with the tenfold [perfections] beginning with omniscience;
it becomes possessed of the *nigarbha*;
and it becomes presided over by Tripuramālinī.
It is endowed with the Mahāṅkuśa mudrā.
The seventh is the wheel that removes all diseases.
It consists of the group of eight beginning with Sarvavaśinī.
It becomes possessed of the secret;
it becomes presided over by the Tripurasiddhi;
it becomes endowed with the Sakhecarī-mudrā.
The eighth is the wheel that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiprada*).
It consists of the fourfold [deities] together with their implements (*sāyudha*).
It contains both the higher and lower secrets (*saparāpararahasya*).
It becomes presided over by Tripurāmbā;
it becomes presided over by the Bījamudrā;
the ninth is the leader of the cakras, the cakra consisting of all-bliss.
The triad beginning with Sakāmeśvarī occurs;
it is the ultimate secret;
it is presided over by Mahātripurasundarī.
It becomes endowed with the *yonimudrā*.
Indeed, all the *chandas* and the *cakras* transition [into it]. That very *cakra* is the *śrīcakra*.
In the circle of fire at his navel are the sun and the moon.

There, having worshipped the Oṃkāra-pīṭha, and having meditated upon the supreme Vidyā in the form of space situated within that syllable which is in the form of a Bindu, one should invoke Mahātripurasundarī:
"O Goddess, bathed with milk, anointed with sandalwood paste,
and honored with Bilva leaves— O Durgā, I have come to you for refuge."
Having thus prayed with this single verse, one should worship Māyālakṣmī by means of the *tantra*; so said the Blessed One.
With these mantras, one should sacrifice to the Goddess;
then the Goddess becomes pleased.
He reveals his own self.
Therefore, he who sacrifices with these mantras sees Brahman;
he sees everything.
He who knows this attains immortality; thus ends the Mahopaniṣad.
Thus ends the second Upaniṣad. || 2 ||
The gods said to the Blessed One, "Let us create the mudrās.
The Blessed One said to them, "Having spread out the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the kneecaps flat on the ground, create the mudrās.
He who masters the yoni-mudrā attracts everyone.
He knows everything;
he enjoys every fruit;
he shatters all things.

It paralyzes one's enemies. Having placed [the hands] with the middle fingers over the ring fingers, and having read from the little fingers and thumbs, the two index fingers are released and positioned below like a staff; such is the first [mudrā]. That same [mudrā], with the middle fingers joined together, becomes the second.

The third is the form of the hook (*aṅkuśa*). Having rubbed the hands together in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), one joins the two thumbs along with their tips; this is the fourth. The little fingers are interlaced, the middle fingers are bound together, and the ring fingers are held like staffs; having embraced and pressed the index fingers, the thumbs are joined at the nails of the middle fingers; this is the fifth.
That same [hand] in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*) first is the sixth.

Having placed the left arm upon the right shoulder, with the two ring fingers interlaced and the two middle fingers positioned between them, the two index fingers pressing down upon them while the thumbs are straight—this is *khecarī*, the seventh.

With all [fingers] raised upward for the withdrawal of all things (*sarvasaṃhṛti*), the two index fingers joined like hooks on the sides of the little fingers within the space between the middle and ring fingers, and having formed a level *añjali* by joining the thumbs together—this is the eighth.

When the two ring fingers, positioned on the back of the middle fingers, are pressed by the index fingers, and the two middle fingers are held level while the two thumbs are placed between them, the ninth [mudrā] is attained.
This same [mudrā], when the two little fingers are made level and separated, and the two thumbs are likewise made level and separated, becomes the *trikhaṇḍā*.
The five arrows and the first five mudrās are thus clearly explained.
*Kromaṅkuśā*, *hasakhphreṃ* is Khecarī; *haṃsrau* is the eighth seed-syllable (*bījāṣṭamī*); the ninth begins with Vāgbhava, and the tenth is thus accomplished.
He who knows thus.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the wheel consisting of the digits of desire (*kāmakalā*). *Hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ blū cṃ srauṃ*—these five desires revolve throughout the entire wheel.

Having encapsulated the central desire at the end of all [the others], and having made the encapsulation pervaded by the syllable *blūṃ*, one binds the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) with the twice-repeated [seed-syllable] of the Moon situated in the center, and worships it on a birch-bark leaf.
He who knows that wheel knows everything;
he attracts all the worlds;
he paralyzes everything.
A wheel joined with indigo kills enemies and paralyzes their movement.
Having prepared it with lac, one brings the entire world under one's control.
Having performed one million recitations (*japa*), one attains the state of Rudra.
Having encircled [the mantra] with the *mātṛkā*, one becomes victorious.
Having prepared a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (*bhagāṅkakuṇḍa*) and established the fire, a man who offers oblations (*havis*) with clarified butter brings women under his control.
Having offered oblations in a circular shape, one attains incomparable prosperity. Having offered oblations in a square shape, rain occurs.
Having offered oblations in a triangular shape, one slays enemies.
It paralyzes movement.
By offering flowers, one becomes victorious.
By offering great essences, one becomes filled with supreme bliss.
"We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of most exalted fame, the supreme king of sacred hymns, O Brahmaṇaspati; hearing us, sit upon your seat with your protections.
With this verse beginning thus and ending with the syllable "Om" (the full-point), he touches the limb.
One should pay homage to Gaṇeśa with the mantra: *gaṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ*.

*Oṃ namo bhagavate bhasmāṅgarāgāyogratejase hanahana daha daha pacapaca mathamatha vidhvaṃsayavidhvaṃsaya halabhañjana śūlamūle vyañjanasiddhiṃ kurukuru samudraṃ pūrvapratiṣṭhitataṃ śoṣayaśoṣaya stambhayastambhaya paramantraparayantraparatantraparadūtaparakaṭakaparacchedanakara vidārayavidāraya cchindhicchindhi hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.*
With this, one should worship the Overseer of the Field (*kṣetrādhyakṣa*).
"O Daughter of the Kula, we know; we meditate upon the one whose intellect is the ten million mantras;
may that Kaulika impel us."
Having thus performed the worship of the maiden, the practitioner who indeed paints [the image] attains immortality;
he obtains fame;
he attains supreme longevity, or else, having pierced through the Supreme Brahman, he remains established therein.
"He who knows thus"—this is the Great Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the third Upaniṣad.
The gods indeed said to the Blessed One: "O Lord, the Gāyatra heart has been explained to us, as well as the Traipura, which is supreme among all.
The eightfold Traipura has been declared to us by means of the Jātavedas hymn;
having worshipped with this, the yogi is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra."
Then, having heard these words of all the gods who were saying, "Now tell us the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra]," he demonstrates the Mṛtyuñjaya by means of the Tryambaka mantra in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Why is it called Tryambaka? Because it is the eye (ambaka) of the three cities, or their master; therefore it is called Tryambaka.
Now, why is it said, "yajāmaha"?

We worship (*yajāmahe*) and we serve (*sevāmahe*) the Reality (*vastu*); by means of the two syllables *ma-ha*, and by means of the single syllable as a *kūṭa*, it is called the "Conqueror of Death" (*mṛtyuñjaya*).
Therefore, it is said, "yajāmaha. Now, why is it said, "sugandhi"?
One attains fame from every side;
therefore it is called "fragrant.
Now, why is it called "the increaser of prosperity"?
Because it creates all the worlds, because it delivers all the worlds, and because it pervades all the worlds, it is therefore called "the Increaser of Prosperity" (*puṣṭivardhana*).
Now, why is it said, "May he release me from death as a cucumber from its stem"?
Because of being attached—like a cucumber—from the bondage of death, that is, from the bondage of *saṃsāra*, because of being attached and bound, one becomes released; one becomes liberated.
Now, why is it said "from me, immortality"? One attains immortality; one attains the Imperishable (akṣara) and becomes Rudra himself.
The gods indeed said to the Blessed One: "Everything has been explained to us.
Now, tell us all those mantras—be they Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, or Gāṇeśa—by which, when praised, the Blessed Goddess reveals her own self."
The Blessed One said: "One should worship Mṛtyuñjaya with the Tryambaka Anuṣṭubh.
It is remembered that the single syllable pervades the eastern path.
The practitioner of the Yajurvedic mantra 'Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya' attains the state of Rudra."
One who knows this attains what is auspicious. "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

Like an eye stretched across the sky, the affection of Viṣṇu—who faces in all directions—pervades like a mass of minced meat, woven in and out, both immanent and transcendent. As he thus pervades, the wise—the gods beginning with Brahmā—behold his supreme station; they gaze upon that supreme station as the highest ether, and they ever hold it within their hearts.
Therefore, because he dwells and abides within all beings as the very form of Viṣṇu, he is called Vāsudeva.
"Oṃ namaḥ" consists of three syllables; "bhagavate" consists of four;
and "vāsudevāya" consists of five syllables.
He who approaches this twelve-syllable mantra of Vāsudeva crosses over all calamities and attains a full lifespan.

He attains the state of Prajāpati and enjoys the abundance of wealth and the prosperity of cattle; he reaches the inward bliss, the Person who is Brahman, whose nature is the syllable *praṇava*—namely, the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. These [letters] become one; that is *oṃ*. "The swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house."
"Seated in men, seated in the best, seated in truth, seated in the sky, born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth.
This [mantra] "Haṃsa," supported by the second syllable of the mind, which is a solar mass of light, [is] "born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth.
By means of the powers of Dawn, Twilight, and Wisdom—possessing the solar mass of light of Satya—one who first studies the solar [mantra] enjoys all fruit.
He dwells in the supreme abode of the sky, in the solar realm.
By worshipping the Lord of the Gaṇas with the *triṣṭubh* verse "gaṇānām" (RV 2.23.1) using the ancient path and the single-syllable *mantra*, one attains the state of Gaṇeśa.
Now, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Ajapā, and Mātṛkā are proclaimed; by her, all this is pervaded.
"Oṃ aiṃ, we know Vāgīśvarī; oṃ klīṃ, we meditate on Kāmeśvarī;
may that Śakti of ours impel us.
This is the Gāyatrī at dawn, the Sāvitrī at midday, and Sarasvatī in the evening; thus it is the incessant ajapā.

The Mother (Mātṛkā) is indeed "Haṃsa. The worlds, the scriptures, and the meters are pervaded by her form consisting of the fifty letters from *a* to *kṣ*. Thus, the Blessed Lady pervades everything; therefore, "Salutations again and again to her! The Blessed One said to them: "He who constantly praises the Goddess with these mantras sees everything."
He who knows thus attains immortality; this is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the Turīyopaniṣad. 4.

The gods indeed said to the Blessed One: "O Lord, you have clearly explained the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) along with its domain, namely the Traipura. Now, please explain the supreme non-differentiated [reality]. To them the Blessed One spoke by means of the fourth and final *māyā*.
It is designated as the Supreme Brahman;

as the Supreme Person, whose nature is consciousness, as the Supreme Self; as the hearer, the thinker, the seer, the ordainer, the toucher, the smeller, the knower, and the perceiver—the inner person within all persons.

"That is the Self; that is to be known. Therein there are no worlds and no non-worlds, no gods and no non-gods, no cattle and no non-cattle, no ascetics and no non-ascetics, no Paulkasas and no non-Paulkasas, no Brahmins and no non-Brahmins. That alone, the one supreme Brahman, shines forth as Nirvana.
Therein, neither the gods, nor the sages, nor the ancestors have power over one who is awakened through all-encompassing knowledge.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
Therefore, the seeker of liberation should make the mind eternally free from objective domains.
For liberation of the mind is held to consist in its being without an object. || 1 ||
The mind is indeed said to be of two kinds: pure and impure.
The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. (2)
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
the mind attached to sense objects leads to bondage, while the mind free from sense objects leads to liberation.
When, having completely restrained the mind within the heart so that its attachment to sense objects is cast away,
it reaches the state of non-mind, then that is the supreme state.
It should be suppressed right then, until it reaches the heart and is destroyed;
this alone is knowledge and meditation—the rest is merely an expansion of books.
Neither conceivable nor inconceivable, neither the object of thought nor indeed not the object of thought—
one who is completely free from partiality certainly attains Brahman.
The yogi should pierce with sound; he should contemplate the supreme sound.
But by means of the state of soundlessness, no state is desired as a state.
That very Brahman is partless, free from conceptual construction, and stainless;
having realized "I am that Brahman," one gradually attains Brahman.
That which is free from conceptual construction, infinite, devoid of causes and examples, immeasurable, and without beginning or end—by knowing that, the wise one is liberated. || 9 ||
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner,
neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated— this is the ultimate reality.
The Self should be understood as one and the same throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
for one who has transcended these three states, rebirth no longer exists.
For the single Self of all beings, though established in every being,
is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
Just as when a jar containing space is being carried away, it is the jar that is carried and not the space; so too is the individual soul (jīva) comparable to the sky. || 13 ||
Though it is repeatedly divided again and again into various forms like a jar,
he does not perceive that division, yet he knows it eternally.
As long as one is enveloped by the illusion of sound, so long does one remain in the state of manifoldness;
but when that darkness is shattered, one perceives oneness alone. || 15 ||
The supreme Brahman is the ocean of sound; when that has ceased, there is the Imperishable.
If one desires peace for oneself, one should meditate upon that Imperishable known by the wise.
For two Brahmans are to be meditated upon: the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (17)
Having studied the scripture, the wise person, intent upon knowledge and realization, should discard the scripture entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (18)

Just as the milk of cows of many different colors is of a single color, so the wise man perceives [the underlying unity] within those who possess external marks, just like the milk [is perceived apart from the cows]. 19.
Having fixed the eye of knowledge, he should contemplate, "I am Brahman"—that great, supreme state which is partless, immovable, and tranquil. (20)

Thus, he who knows this one form of the Supreme Brahman, the abode of all beings, the fourth state (turīya), dwells in the imperishable, supreme ether. I take refuge here for the sake of my life-span in that fourth knowledge, which is the very nature of the womb of Brahman.
I take refuge. Space is the ultimate resort of all these beings in the sequence beginning with space. Indeed, all these beings are born from space alone;
they merge into space alone; from that alone they are born and live. Therefore, it is born from space.

One should know the seed-syllable (*bīja*). One should understand that very [seed-syllable] as the seat of space (*ākāśapīṭha*), the seat of touch (*spārśanapīṭha*), the seat of fire (*tejaḥpīṭha*), the seat of nectar (*amṛtapīṭha*), and the seat of jewels (*ratnapīṭha*). He who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, one should [know] this fourth [syllable], the Śrīkāmarājīyā, in eleven ways.
He who knows that Brahman is the single syllable when it is differentiated attains the fourth state (*turiya*);
"He who knows thus"—this is the Great Upanishad.
Thus ends the fifth Upaniṣad. || 5 ||
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, we have offered praise; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel is unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Hariḥ Oṃ, that is the Truth.
Thus ends the venerable Tripurātāpinī Upaniṣad.
